title: Room Preference as a Function of Architectural Features and User Activities

findings.antecedent: architectural features (ceiling height, ceiling slope, wall angle)
findings.mechanism: parametric variation of architectural features leads to different mean preference ratings.
findings.quote: Parametric variation of each feature clearly led to different mean ratings

findings.mechanism: variations in ceiling height significantly affect preference, showing a single-peaked function.
findings.quote: ceiling height, F(7, 203) = 21.2, p < .001

findings.mechanism: the relationship between perceived ceiling height (logarithm of actual height) and preference can be described by a quadratic equation, indicating a peak preference.
findings.quote: The coefficient of determination (r²) between observed and theoretical values (after the fit) is .98.

findings.mechanism: preference for ceiling height shows a single peak, with 10 feet being the most desirable.
findings.quote: there is a single-peaked preference with a maximum of 10 feet (3.04 m)

findings.antecedent: ceiling height (lower or higher than 10 ft)
findings.mechanism: deviations from the optimal ceiling height of 10 feet lead to reduced preference.
findings.quote: lower or higher ceilings were less desirable.

findings.mechanism: preference declines more gradually when ceiling height increases beyond the optimal point compared to when it decreases below it.
findings.quote: preference decreases more gradually on the higher side of the peak.

findings.mechanism: variations in ceiling slope significantly affect preference, showing a double-peaked function.
findings.quote: ceiling slope, F(6, 174) = 6.7, p < .001

findings.mechanism: preference for ceiling slope exhibits two peaks, one for a horizontal ceiling and another for an intermediate slope.
findings.quote: The preference for ceiling slope has two peaks, one for the horizontal plane (0°) and the other for an intermediate slope of 4/12.

findings.mechanism: a slight deviation from a horizontal ceiling is negatively perceived.
findings.quote: There appears to be a negative reaction to a slope just off square (1/12)

findings.mechanism: variations in wall angle significantly affect preference, showing a single-peaked function.
90-degree wall angles are most preferred, with wider angles also being acceptable.
findings.quote: Although 90° is most preferred, wider angles were also acceptable.

findings.mechanism: acute wall angles are rated negatively.
findings.quote: Acute angles are rated negatively.

findings.mechanism: the order of stimulus presentation did not significantly influence preference ratings.
findings.quote: Neither trials nor its interaction with the particular architectural feature was significant.

findings.mechanism: ceiling height significantly affects preference, accounting for 16% of the variance.
findings.quote: effect of ceiling height was significant, F(7, 1160) = 38, p < .05, but activity was not. The main effect accounted for 16% of the variance.

findings.antecedent: user activity (reading, dancing, dining, talking, listening) (Experiment 2)
findings.mechanism: the main effect of user activity on preference was not significant.
findings.quote: activity was not [significant].

findings.antecedent: ceiling height x user activity interaction (Experiment 2)
findings.mechanism: the effect of ceiling height on preference varies depending on the user activity, accounting for 7% of the variance.
findings.quote: The interaction between ceiling height and activity was also significant, F(28, 1160) = 5, p < .05, accounting for 7% of the variance.

findings.mechanism: subjects prefer higher ceilings when engaged in listening activities, possibly due to the public nature of the activity.
findings.quote: subjects preferred higher ceilings for the listening activity.

findings.mechanism: variations in ceiling height in a physical space significantly affect preference, accounting for 42% of the variance.
findings.quote: The main effect of height was significant, F(7,87) = 23.6, p < .001, but activity was not. The interaction between height and activity was also significant, F(7,84) = 5.4, p < .001, although it only accounted for 6% of the variance (as compared with 42% for height).

findings.mechanism: the main effect of user activity on preference was not significant in the physical space condition.
findings.quote: activity was not [significant].

findings.antecedent: ceiling height x user activity interaction (Experiment 3)
findings.mechanism: the effect of ceiling height on preference varies depending on the user activity, accounting for 6% of the variance in the physical space condition.
findings.quote: The interaction between height and activity was also significant, F(7,84) = 5.4, p < .001, although it only accounted for 6% of the variance

findings.antecedent: adjustable ceiling (physical space) vs. model rooms
findings.consequent: subjects' preference sensitivity to ceiling height changes
findings.mechanism: direct experience with a physical adjustable ceiling leads to more sensitive preference ratings compared to viewing model rooms.
findings.quote: subjects' preferences were more sensitive to changes in the adjustable ceiling than they were to changes in the models.

findings.mechanism: people generally prefer ceilings that are higher than what is commonly found in existing buildings.
findings.quote: people in our experiments prefer higher ceilings than those usually encountered in the environment.

findings.mechanism: intermediate ceiling slopes within this range are most preferred.
findings.quote: The most preferred slopes were between 3/12 and 5/12 pitch.

stimuli.description: white fiberboard scale models of rooms with varying ceiling height (6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15 ft), ceiling slope (0, 1/12, 2/12, 3/12, 4/12, 5/12, 6/12 pitch), and wall angle (45°, 67.5°, 90°, 112.5°, 135°). A scale model of a woman was included for scale reference.
a 3x3 ft fiberboard ceiling adjustable to heights of 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15 feet in a physical setup, allowing subjects to walk beneath it.

limitations: Suggestions apply best to the range of architectural levels employed and should be extrapolated to other levels with care.

Individual differences were substantial, and although the bulk of this variance was attributed to subjects' use of the rating scale, the relative contribution of this factor and actual differences in individual preference were not established.
Subjects were Dartmouth undergraduates, whose preferences may not match those of other populations.
